summary:
Moon Base 30 is a pixel-art survival game where students run a lunar outpost for 30 days. Players launch from Earth, land on the Moon, and keep a crew of two to four alive by balancing oxygen, water, food, power, radiation, hull integrity and health. Each day offers only a few actions, so players must choose: more power for making oxygen means less for the greenhouse, and more spacewalks for science means more radiation. Crew roles (doctor, engineer, biologist, geologist), three difficulty levels, a lunar night, dust storms, solar flares and supply ships make every run different.

The game answers the challenge by turning real engineering trade-offs into tangible, fun decisions for young learners. Science missions with quizzes based on NASA facts, an astronaut passport with achievements, and a final debrief explain the real-world trade-off behind each result. This matters because space missions are decided by trade-offs, not single right answers, and students who feel those choices early understand why missions succeed or fail. The game runs in a browser in English and Russian.
details:
What it does and how it works

Moon Base 30 is a browser-based pixel-art game. The player picks a difficulty (Easy, Medium, Hard) and a crew of two to four astronauts: doctor, engineer, biologist or geologist. After a short launch and landing sequence, the player manages the base for 30 days. Each day the crew has a limited number of actions: repair the habitat, make oxygen from lunar soil, mine water ice, tend the greenhouse, add radiation shielding, explore the surface, clean the solar panels, exercise, or call home. When the player ends the day, a simulation updates seven resources (oxygen, water, food, power, hull, radiation, health). It also triggers events: a lunar night, dust storms, solar flares, micrometeorites, equipment faults and supply ships. Roles give bonuses (for example, engineers repair twice as fast and biologists grow more food), and the harder the difficulty, the scarcer the supplies and the stronger the storms and radiation.

Learning and benefits

Because actions are limited, the player can never fix everything. A good result needs planning, such as saving power before the lunar night or building shielding early. Science missions ask short quiz questions about real space topics. An astronaut passport records achievements, and a local leaderboard encourages replay. At the end, a debrief shows a chart of resources by day and explains the real-world trade-off behind the player’s weakest resource, for example power versus life support or shielding versus mobility.

Intended impact

We want students aged about 10 to 15 to understand that space missions are decided by trade-offs, not single correct answers, and to feel why life support, power, food and radiation are connected. The game is free, runs in a browser without installation, and supports English and Russian, so teachers and students can use it easily.

Tools and technology

  • Web version: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, HTML Canvas for the pixel scene, Web Audio API for sound.
  • Godot 4 and GDScript: a 2D pixel-art version is in development, with balance data in JSON and translations in CSV.
  • Claude (Anthropic): design ideas, balance prototyping and code drafts.
  • Facts in the game are based on NASA material about the ISS, the Artemis program, lunar surface conditions and space radiation.Game numbers are simplified for learning and are not real mission data.

Creativity

Instead of a quiz or a fixed simulation, we made a short story of choices: the crew roles, limited actions and visible consequences on the pixel base (lights go out, cracks appear, plants grow, astronauts get tired). The final debrief connects the player’s result to a real engineering trade-off.

Factors we considered

  • Keeping it simple enough for young players but not misleading about how real missions work.
  • Balancing difficulty so that survival is possible on Easy and demanding on Hard.
  • Honesty about simplified numbers and about our use of AI tools.
  • Accessibility and reach: no installation, two languages, readable text and controls.
